title: Lesson 82: Change Management: Training, Adoption, and Feedback Loops
description: Separating training, adoption and reinforcement as three jobs with three artifacts, the published evidence on resistance and proficiency, the 1:3:5 spend pattern, coaching over one-time training, a proficiency gate on real cases, adoption telemetry built on speed, utilization and proficiency, the weekly loop that turns corrections into eval cases, reinforcement and stopping rules, and a 90-day program for the invoice exception queue.

questions.question: A program has spent 180,000 dollars on the agent build and the ERP integration, 3,000 dollars a month on run and eval upkeep, and has no budget line for process redesign or capability building. Per the lesson, what does this spend shape indicate?
options: The program is in good shape, because the payback math from the invoice queue case does not depend on training spend
The build line is underweighted, so the auto-clear rate will stay below the 40 percent design assumption
The program is buying a capability it has not decided how to absorb, because capability building was treated as an implementation detail while technology took the money and attention
The ratio is correct, since the one to three to five pattern applies only to programs with a budget above one million dollars
questions.explanation: The lesson states the 1:3:5 finding as a diagnostic rather than a budget rule: if technology is the largest of the three numbers, the program is buying a capability it has not decided how to absorb, and it applies that reading directly to the 180,000 dollar build with no line for redesign or capability building.

questions.question: The AP lead reports that all six analysts finished the two-hour training session and asks whether the team is ready for go-live. According to the lesson, what is still missing?
options: A completion dashboard with per-analyst timestamps, so the sponsor can see the training landed

A proficiency gate: twenty real cases including the ugly ones, decisions scored by a reviewer against a stated threshold, a written note on deliberate departures, and a dated retry path for anyone who fails
A follow-up class scheduled thirty days after go-live to refresh the material once people have used the tool
Nothing, because finishing the session closes the knowledge stage and the ability stage follows automatically with practice
questions.explanation: The lesson argues the gap sits between knowledge and ability, that training completion indicates information was received rather than that it can be applied under real conditions, and it lists the four parts of a working gate: real evidence set, scored dry run, stated threshold, retry path with a date.

questions.question: A team has run the weekly triage for eight weeks and produced meeting notes every time, with no eval cases, no policy changes and no tool fixes. Per the lesson, what is happening and what is the fix?
options: The agent is performing well enough that no changes are needed, so the meetings should continue as passive monitoring
The intake schema needs more free-text fields, so analysts can describe problems in richer detail
The loop is capturing without closing, and the fix is to promote at least one corrected answer into the offline eval set each week and require it to be named in the notes
Triage should move to a monthly cadence so each item has time to mature before a decision is made
questions.explanation: The lesson treats the output of a feedback loop as a change to the system, calls a loop with zero conversions for two weeks decorative, and prescribes exactly that fix: promote at least one corrected answer into the offline eval set and name it, since the corrected answer is the field that becomes a test case.
